web_title: 1. Origin, Corporate Evolution & Past Business Cycles
book_title: Chapter 1: How AbbVie Was Built — From Humira Concentration to Post-LOE Reinvention
question: How did AbbVie survive the largest patent cliff in pharmaceutical history, and what structural scars or strengths did those pivots leave behind?

epigraph.quote: We delivered record net sales in just the second full year following the U.S. Humira loss of exclusivity, underscoring the strength of our diversified growth platform.
epigraph.author: Robert A. Michael, Chairman and CEO, AbbVie (FY2025 Results Release, February 2026)

web_blocks.title: The 2013 Abbott Spin-Off and the Humira Concentration Paradox

web_blocks.html: AbbVie Inc. became an independent, publicly traded biopharmaceutical company on January 1, 2013 [1, 24]. On that date, Abbott Laboratories separated its proprietary pharmaceutical division from its medical devices, diagnostics, and nutrition units [1, 24]. At birth, AbbVie inherited one extraordinary asset: Humira (adalimumab), a fully human anti-TNF-alpha monoclonal antibody. Abbott had originally acquired the drug when it bought Knoll Pharmaceuticals in 2001. Humira was a clinical and commercial marvel. Its label expanded across rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis, psoriatic arthritis, Crohn's disease, and ulcerative colitis. Yet that very success created an existential concentration paradox. By 2019, Humira generated about 58% of AbbVie's $33.27B in total net sales [10, 23]. At its peak in 2022, global Humira sales reached $21.24B [10, 23]. U.S. composition-of-matter and formulation patents were set to yield to biosimilars in January 2023. Investors knew AbbVie would then face the steepest single-drug revenue cliff in pharmaceutical history.

Between 2013 and 2022, management executed a two-pronged strategy to buy time and build replacement engines. First, AbbVie built a dense patent estate around Humira's manufacturing processes, formulations, and dosing regimens [10, 24]. Settlement deals with biosimilar challengers delayed U.S. entry until January 2023. That was nearly five years after European biosimilars launched in October 2018 [10, 24]. Second, the company used Humira's massive operating cash flows to fund both internal immunology R&D and transformative external acquisitions. That spending began in 2015 with the $21.0B purchase of Pharmacyclics, which added the BTK inhibitor Imbruvica to oncology [1, 24]. It peaked on May 8, 2020, when AbbVie closed the $63.0B acquisition of Allergan [1, 24].

web_blocks.title: The 2020 Allergan Mega-Deal and the 2023 U.S. Patent Cliff

web_blocks.html: Buying Allergan transformed AbbVie's revenue base overnight. Total annual net sales jumped from $33.27B in 2019 to $45.80B in 2020 and $56.20B in 2021 [23]. Allergan brought Botox, split between Therapeutic neurology and Cosmetic aesthetics, plus the Juvederm dermal filler line. It also added the psychiatry drug Vraylar, the acute migraine therapy Ubrelvy, and an eye-care unit. The goal was diversification. Management diluted Humira from 58% of sales down toward 37% before the 2023 U.S. cliff arrived [10, 23]. The trade-off was a heavy debt load and tens of billions in acquired intangibles and goodwill. That deal permanently reshaped AbbVie's balance sheet and GAAP amortization profile [1, 22].

Even more consequential than Allergan was AbbVie's internal and partnered immunology succession plan. In 2016, AbbVie licensed risankizumab (Skyrizi) from Boehringer Ingelheim for $595M upfront plus milestones and royalties. At the same time, it advanced its internal selective JAK1 inhibitor upadacitinib (Rinvoq). Both drugs won initial FDA approvals in 2019. That gave AbbVie a four-year commercial runway before U.S. Humira biosimilars arrived in 2023. When the cliff hit in 2023, Humira plunged 32.2% to $14.40B [10, 23]. Consolidated revenue fell 6.4% from $58.05B in 2022 to a trough of $54.32B in 2023 [23]. Yet the trough lasted exactly one year. By 2024, Skyrizi and Rinvoq combined to offset Humira's erosion, lifting total revenue to $56.33B (+3.7% YoY). In 2025, total net sales surged 8.6% to a record $61.16B, even as Humira fell to $4.54B [2, 23]. Through the first nine months of 2026, sales reached $49.40B (+10.9% YoY). Full-year 2026 revenue is on track for ~$67.8B [3].

web_blocks.takeaway: AbbVie absorbed a $16.7B cumulative drop in annual Humira sales between 2022 and 2025 while expanding consolidated net revenues to an all-time high of $61.16B in FY2025 and $49.40B in 9M 2026 [2, 3, 23].

web_blocks.title: 2024–2026: Reloading the Pipeline Beyond 2030 and Learning from M&A Misses

web_blocks.html: With Skyrizi and Rinvoq driving near-term growth, AbbVie turned to its 2030s pipeline. Management favored targeted bolt-on deals over mega-mergers. In February 2024, AbbVie closed the $10.1B purchase of ImmunoGen [13]. That deal brought Elahere, the first FDA-approved folate receptor-alpha ADC for platinum-resistant ovarian cancer [13]. In August 2024, AbbVie completed the $8.7B acquisition of Cerevel Therapeutics to bolster neuroscience [14]. That deal delivered a sharp lesson in clinical risk. In November 2024, Cerevel's lead schizophrenia drug emraclidine failed two Phase 2 trials (EMPOWER-1 and EMPOWER-2) against placebo [14, 15]. AbbVie recorded a $4.48B pre-tax ($3.51B after-tax) intangible impairment in Q4 2024 [2]. Even so, Cerevel's selective D1/D5 agonist tavapadon (Juvmo) succeeded in Phase 3. It won FDA approval for Parkinson's disease in Q3 2026 [3, 7].

Rather than retreating after the emraclidine setback, AbbVie continued deploying cash into next-generation immunology and solid-tumor modalities. In 2025, it bought Nimble Therapeutics and Capstan Therapeutics ($2.1B cash) for in vivo CAR-T autoimmune drugs [2, 12]. It also licensed PD-1/VEGF bispecific antibody RC148 (ABBV-1480) from RemeGen and an amylin obesity analog (ABBV-295) from Gubra [2]. In September 2026, AbbVie closed its $10.9B buyout of Apogee Therapeutics [3, 11]. That added half-life-extended IL-13 antibody zumilokibart for atopic dermatitis and an IL-13/TSLP bispecific for asthma [11]. GAAP operating margins fell to a 16.2% trough in 2024 due to the emraclidine write-down [2, 23]. Margins then rebounded to 24.6% in 2025 and 33.8% in 9M 2026. High-margin Skyrizi and Rinvoq sales scaled well past fixed commercial overhead [3]. Across all four cycles, AbbVie's defining trait has been capital velocity. Management recycles cash from peaking blockbusters into external science years before patent cliffs hit. It accepts higher debt and GAAP amortization drag to avoid multi-year revenue drops.

web_blocks.mechanism: Facing a rapid revenue cliff in its dominant Hepatitis C (HCV) franchise (Sovaldi/Harvoni), Gilead spent over $30B on external oncology M&A. Those deals included Kite Pharma for $11.9B and Immunomedics for $21.0B. However, Gilead lacked an internal multi-indication organic engine like Skyrizi and Rinvoq.
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: Gilead's total revenue fell from $32.6B in 2015 to $22.4B in 2019 and stagnated near $27B through 2023. The company also took multi-billion-dollar impairment charges on acquired oncology assets, including Trodelvy and Galapagos write-downs.
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: External M&A cannot replace a strong internal or partnered clinical platform. AbbVie's $3.5B emraclidine write-down proves AbbVie is not immune to clinical failure. Because Skyrizi and Rinvoq already replaced Humira organically, Cerevel's miss was an accounting scar rather than a revenue crisis.

web_blocks.title: What This Evolution Means for an Owner
paragraphs: AbbVie's 13-year history shows that a drugmaker can survive a $16B+ flagship patent cliff under strict conditions. Replacement molecules must be clinically superior, not me-too line extensions, and launch three to four years before exclusivity ends. Still, the 2020 Allergan and 2024 Cerevel deals left behind $67.5B in year-end 2025 debt. They also showed that acquired Phase 2 science carries binary impairment risk. Owners must weigh AbbVie's strong commercial engine against the balance-sheet cost of serial dealmaking. Next, we break down the five commercial franchises generating AbbVie's $61.2B revenue base today.

book_paragraphs: When Abbott Laboratories spun off AbbVie on January 1, 2013, skeptics saw a single-product cash cow on borrowed time. Abbott kept the steady medical devices, diagnostics, and nutrition businesses. It handed the new company a blockbuster immunology drug called Humira plus a handful of older specialty drugs. Even then, Humira made up roughly half of AbbVie's sales. That share climbed as doctors prescribed the drug across nearly a dozen autoimmune diseases. By 2019, Humira generated 58 percent of AbbVie's $33.27 billion in annual sales. By 2022, it reached a global peak of $21.24 billion. Every healthcare investor knew the math. When U.S. biosimilars arrived in January 2023, AbbVie would face the largest single-drug patent cliff in industry history.

AbbVie beat peers that stumbled over similar cliffs through a disciplined, decade-long plan. Management executed across two phases: buying time with patents and buying scale with cash flow. First, AbbVie built a multi-layered patent wall around Humira's manufacturing methods, citrate-free formula, and dosing schedules. That legal defense won settlements with biosimilar rivals. Those deals kept U.S. copycats off the market until January 2023, five years after European biosimilars launched in late 2018. Those five extra years of U.S. exclusivity generated tens of billions of dollars in operating cash flow.

Second, management refused to sit idle on that cash. In 2015, AbbVie paid $21 billion for Pharmacyclics to gain half the global profits of Imbruvica in blood cancer. In 2016, it paid Boehringer Ingelheim $595 million upfront for rights to risankizumab, an IL-23 antibody that became Skyrizi. Meanwhile, it advanced its own internal JAK1 inhibitor, upadacitinib, which became Rinvoq. Both Skyrizi and Rinvoq won FDA approval in 2019—four full years before U.S. Humira biosimilars launched. Then, in May 2020, AbbVie closed the $63 billion buyout of Allergan, adding Botox, Juvederm, Vraylar, and Ubrelvy. That single deal lifted AbbVie's annual revenue from $33.27 billion in 2019 to $56.20 billion by 2021. It diluted Humira's share of sales well before the 2023 storm arrived.

Not every capital bet worked along the way. In 2014, AbbVie tried a $54 billion tax-inversion merger with Shire. It walked away after U.S. Treasury rules changed, paying a $1.64 billion breakup fee that hurt 2014 margins. Two years later, AbbVie spent $5.8 billion upfront to buy Stemcentrx for Rova-T, an experimental lung cancer drug. Rova-T failed in late-stage trials and was written off in 2019. Those early misses taught management a lasting lesson. Megadeals for tax savings or unproven single-asset biotechs destroy capital, while proven franchises in core disease areas compound value. That capital-allocation discipline shaped every deal AbbVie pursued over the next seven years.

book_subsections.title: Surviving the 2023 Cliff and Returning to Record Scale
paragraphs: Eight U.S. Humira biosimilars finally launched in 2023. Humira's global sales dropped 32.2 percent to $14.40 billion, pulling AbbVie's total revenue down 6.4 percent from $58.05 billion in 2022 to $54.32 billion. Most drugmakers take half a decade to recover from a drop that steep. AbbVie's trough lasted twelve months. In 2024, Humira fell another 37.5 percent to roughly $9.0 billion. Yet total company revenue still grew 3.7 percent to $56.33 billion. Skyrizi and Rinvoq scaled rapidly across psoriasis, psoriatic arthritis, Crohn's disease, and ulcerative colitis. Doctors adopted both therapies quickly because head-to-head trials proved clear clinical gains.

By 2025, the crossover was decisive. Humira fell by half again to $4.54 billion, yet AbbVie posted record net sales of $61.16 billion, up 8.6 percent. Skyrizi alone generated $17.56 billion—over four times Humira's remaining sales—while Rinvoq added $8.30 billion. That momentum sped up in 2026. Nine-month net sales hit $49.40 billion, up 10.9 percent year over year. Management guided full-year 2026 revenue to roughly $67.8 billion. Less than three years after losing U.S. exclusivity on a $21 billion drug, AbbVie had built a larger, faster-growing business.

The profit math behind that recovery matters as much as the sales headline. AbbVie sold Skyrizi and Rinvoq through the exact same immunology salesforce, medical teams, and payer contracts that supported Humira. As a result, new revenue dropped through at very high margins. When high-margin U.S. Humira volume vanished in 2023, GAAP operating margins compressed from 31.2 percent in 2022 to 23.5 percent. Once Skyrizi and Rinvoq crossed $25 billion combined in 2025, operating leverage snapped back. Combined sales pushed past a $32 billion run-rate in 2026, lifting nine-month GAAP operating margin to 33.8 percent. Reusing existing commercial teams kept selling costs flat while revenue surged.

callouts.title: Why Replacement Beat Defense
callouts.text: Patent walls only delay erosion; they never cure it. AbbVie survived because its new drugs were clinically better. Skyrizi showed higher skin-clearance rates than Humira in head-to-head psoriasis trials. Rinvoq offered oral convenience and deep remission in bowel disease. Doctors switched patients willingly before biosimilars even arrived.

book_subsections.title: The 2024–2026 M&A Cycle and the Emraclidine Reality Check
paragraphs: With near-term growth secure, AbbVie turned to the post-2033 horizon, when Skyrizi and Rinvoq will face their own patent cliffs. Instead of another debt-heavy mega-merger like Allergan, management pursued $2 billion to $11 billion bolt-on deals. Those deals targeted solid-tumor oncology, immunology, and neuroscience. In February 2024, AbbVie closed the $10.1 billion purchase of ImmunoGen, adding the ovarian cancer drug Elahere. Six months later, it closed the $8.7 billion buyout of Cerevel Therapeutics. That deal bet heavily on emraclidine, a muscarinic M4 drug for schizophrenia. Management hoped Cerevel would anchor a third major neuroscience growth leg.

The Cerevel deal delivered a fast lesson in drug-development odds. In November 2024, emraclidine failed to beat placebo in two Phase 2 schizophrenia trials. AbbVie had to write down $4.48 billion pre-tax ($3.51 billion after-tax) in the fourth quarter of 2024. That charge pushed full-year GAAP operating margin down to 16.2 percent. AbbVie later salvaged value from Cerevel when tavapadon (Juvmo) won FDA approval for Parkinson's disease in late 2026. It is also re-testing emraclidine at a five-fold higher 150 milligram dose. Still, the miss showed that even disciplined buyers can misread Phase 2 brain biology.

The contrast with Gilead Sciences is instructive. After Gilead's Hepatitis C franchise peaked in 2015, it spent over $30 billion on external cancer deals, including Kite Pharma and Immunomedics. Yet Gilead lacked an internal multi-indication growth engine to cushion the transition. Its revenue stagnated for nearly a decade as acquired assets took repeated write-downs. AbbVie's Cerevel impairment hurt on paper. However, because Skyrizi and Rinvoq were already growing 25 to 50 percent organically, the emraclidine miss stayed an accounting charge rather than a crisis.

Unfazed, AbbVie kept putting free cash flow into external science in 2025 and 2026. It bought Capstan Therapeutics for up to $2.1 billion to enter in vivo CAR-T autoimmune therapy. It also licensed a PD-1/VEGF bispecific from RemeGen and an obesity amylin analog from Gubra. In September 2026, AbbVie closed its $10.9 billion buyout of Apogee Therapeutics for long-acting eczema and asthma antibodies. GAAP operating margins rebounded to 24.6 percent in 2025 and 33.8 percent in the first nine months of 2026. High-margin immunology volume easily absorbed fixed commercial overhead. The core engine is humming, though the balance sheet still holds heavy debt and intangibles from serial dealmaking. Next, we examine what each of AbbVie's five commercial franchises actually sells and earns.
